meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are decades where nothing happens; and there are weeks where decades happen'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Lenin. First credited to him in a 2001 Guardian column, 77 years after his death. A closer version was printed in a 1908 novel.

answer.label: Not Lenin — no source in anything he wrote
answer.authorDates: Earliest known appearance in print: 20 October 2001
answer.sourceLine: Neither Quote Investigator ↗ nor Snopes ↗ can find these words in Lenin’s writings or recorded speeches. The earliest citation crediting him is a Guardian column by MP George Galloway published on 20 October 2001 — 77 years after Lenin’s death — and closer-sounding variants were already in print in 1908 and 1991 with no connection to him at all.

source.heading: Where the sentence actually first appears

docMeta.dd: George Galloway MP — who credited it to Lenin

source.excerpt: In exile in Switzerland, shortly before the Russian revolution, Lenin opined that “there are decades when nothing happens; and there are weeks when decades happen”. We are, it seems, living through such weeks. It is hard to remember a time when political instability, civil strife and the roar of bombs and missiles have so scarred the international landscape.
trail: Lenin died on 21 January 1924. Quote Investigator ↗ reports that the earliest citation ascribing this remark to him appeared in 2001, and says the long delay “greatly reduced the credibility of the ascription to Lenin.”

The nearest genuine Lenin text is “The Chief Task of Our Day” ↗, written 11 March 1918 and first published in Izvestia the next day. The relevant passage is three sentences long and reads as argument, not epigram.

Snopes ↗ found a closer antecedent published during Lenin’s lifetime: in Adriaan Schade van Westrum’s 1908 novel The Devil, a character says “There are years, centuries, in which nothing happens, and there are days, like yesterday, into which a whole lifetime is compressed.” That sentence is in the scanned text ↗, and nothing connects it to Lenin.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its Misattributed section, dating the misattribution to Galloway’s 2001 column.
source.excerptNote: This is the opening of Galloway’s column, and the earliest known appearance of the wording anywhere — though his text reads “when… when,” and the “where… where” form now in circulation is a later drift. Note that the attribution arrives with no citation of its own — just “Lenin opined” — and no scholar has since found the source Galloway implied.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted, because no author or source work has ever been identified for this wording. The line cannot be tied to any work by Lenin, so it is not covered by anything in his public-domain corpus; the earliest text that demonstrably contains it is a 2001 newspaper column, which is itself in copyright. Treat the sentence as an unsourced modern saying rather than a public-domain quotation.

author.name: Vladimir Lenin
author.heading: So who was Lenin, and why does this stick to him?
author.metaLine: 1870–1924 · Russian revolutionary and founding head of Soviet Russia
author.bio: Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, known as Lenin, led the Bolsheviks to power in the October Revolution of 1917 and headed the new Soviet state until his death in January 1924. He wrote constantly and at length — pamphlets, polemics, newspaper columns — which is exactly why a punchy line about history speeding up sounds like something he could have produced. He did write about revolutionary time compressing, but never like this: his own 1918 version runs to three sentences and reads nothing like an aphorism.

cite.sourceCitation: Galloway, George. “We will not be silenced.” The Guardian (London), 20 October 2001, p. 22. No source for this wording has been found in Lenin’s writings or recorded speeches; see “Quote Origin: Days Into Which 20 Years Are Compressed,” Quote Investigator, 13 July 2020.

misattribution.heading: The paper trail runs backwards
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most reliably misattributed sentences on the internet — quoted in newspapers, in a 2014 medical journal editorial, and in Billy Idol’s memoir. Here is who gets the credit, and who has any claim to it.

items.why: Lenin died in January 1924. The earliest citation crediting him that Quote Investigator can find is from 2001 ↗, and Wikiquote lists the line under Misattributed as “not found in Lenin’s writings or recorded speeches.”

His Guardian piece opens: “In exile in Switzerland, shortly before the Russian revolution, Lenin opined that…” ↗ — the first appearance of this wording on record. Galloway used it again in 2009 with no attribution at all.

Lenin really did write about revolutionary time compressing, in “The Chief Task of Our Day” (1918) ↗: “In the space of a few days we destroyed one of the oldest… monarchies. In the space of a few months we passed through a number of stages… for which other countries have required decades.” Quote Investigator calls this a partial match, not a strong one.
By 2020 the saying was being handed to Bannon instead — Quote Investigator cites a Montgomery Advertiser op-ed ↗ calling it something he is “known for saying.”

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody has found an author. Quote Investigator’s verdict is that the origin of this saying remains uncertain ↗ — the honest answer is that the sentence has a long family of near-relatives and no documented parent, and Lenin is not it.

context.heading: Why this one travels so well
lead: The sentence is built to be quoted. It has a hinge in the middle, a reversal on either side, and it flatters whoever deploys it — you only reach for it when you believe you are living through one of the fast weeks. That makes it irresistible in a crisis, and crises are exactly when nobody stops to check a citation.

Attaching it to Lenin does a second job: it makes the observation sound like it comes from someone who actually made history move. But the trail runs the other way. The words show up first in the mouth of a British MP arguing against a war in 2001, and the closest earlier phrasings belong to a forgotten novel and a Mexican poet talking about 1492.
detailsBody: 1863 — Karl Marx, in a letter to Engels dated 9 April, writes of “days into which 20 years are compressed.” Quote Investigator cites the English translation published in Marx & Engels Collected Works, vol. 41 (1985), and notes the passage is neither concise nor close in wording.

1908 — In Adriaan Schade van Westrum’s novel The Devil, the character Jolan says: “There are years, centuries, in which nothing happens, and there are days, like yesterday, into which a whole lifetime is compressed.” This is the closest antecedent, and it was published while Lenin was alive.
1918 — Lenin’s real, documented version, from The Chief Task of Our Day: three sentences about days, months and weeks doing the work of decades. Thematically related; not the quote.

1991 — The poet Homero Aridjis tells the Christian Science Monitor: “There are centuries in which nothing happens and years in which centuries pass.” Snopes traces the line to his poem “Sefarad, 1492.”

2001 — George Galloway opens a Guardian column with the modern wording and hands it to Lenin. Within a month the US columnist Liz Smith is using it as an epigraph, credited the same way; The Scotsman follows in 2003.
context.pull: It is a sentence about history accelerating, and it took 77 years to catch up with the man it is pinned on.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the origin of the saying remains uncertain; Lenin died in 1924 but the earliest citation attributing it to him appeared in 2001 (George Galloway, The Guardian, 20 October 2001, p. 22); Marx's 9 April 1863 letter to Engels contains "days into which 20 years are compressed" (English translation published 1985, MECW vol. 41); Lenin's 1918 "The Chief Task of Our Day" is a partial not strong match; Liz Smith used it in November 2001 and The Scotsman in 2003; a 2020 Montgomery Advertiser op-ed credited it to Steve Bannon; Galloway reused it without attribution in 2009.

Snopes rates the claim "Incorrect Attribution", states there is no evidence Lenin ever spoke or wrote the words, notes it was first attributed to him in 2001 "77 years after the Russian revolutionary's death" in a Guardian op-ed by George Galloway, and documents a closer 1908 antecedent in Adriaan Schade van Westrum's novel The Devil: "There are years, centuries, in which nothing happens, and there are days, like yesterday, into which a whole lifetime is compressed." It also traces the 1991 Aridjis line to his poem "Sefarad, 1492" and cites a 1982 David Eddings variant, Billy Idol's memoir, and a Journal of Hepatology editorial.

Wikiquote lists "There are decades when nothing happens; and there are weeks when decades happen" under its Misattributed section for Vladimir Lenin, states it was first misattributed to Lenin in 2001 in Galloway's Guardian piece "We will not be silenced", and says it is "Not found in Lenin's writings or recorded speeches"; it also notes the 2 Peter 3:8 construction and Marx's 1863 form.

Lenin's "The Chief Task of Our Day" was written 11 March 1918 and first published in Izvestia VTsIK No. 46 on 12 March 1918, and contains: "In the space of a few days we destroyed one of the oldest, most powerful, barbarous and brutal of monarchies. In the space of a few months we passed through a number of stages of collaboration with the bourgeoisie and of shaking off petty-bourgeois illusions, for which other countries have required decades. In the course of a few weeks, having overthrown the bourgeoisie, we crushed its open resistance in civil war."

George Galloway's Guardian column "We will not be silenced" opens: "In exile in Switzerland, shortly before the Russian revolution, Lenin opined that 'there are decades when nothing happens; and there are weeks when decades happen'. We are, it seems, living through such weeks. It is hard to remember a time when political instability, civil strife and the roar of bombs and missiles have so scarred the international landscape."

The scanned full text of Adriaan Schade van Westrum's 1908 novel The Devil contains the sentence, spoken by the character Jolan: "There are years, centuries, in which nothing happens, and there are days, like yesterday, into which a whole lifetime is compressed."

The Christian Science Monitor article "Mexican Novelist Sees 1492 As 'A Year of Centuries'" by David Clark Scott, dated 11 October 1991, quotes Homero Aridjis saying: "There are centuries in which nothing happens and years in which centuries pass. Fourteen ninety-two is a year of centuries."

Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, known as Vladimir Lenin, lived 22 April 1870 to 21 January 1924 and was a Russian revolutionary, politician and political theorist who was the founding head of government of Soviet Russia.
